courseTitle: 3D Gaussian splatting: real-time radiance fields from photos
lessonTitle: Anatomy of a Gaussian: position, covariance, opacity, SH color
md: Opacity is not the alpha used in blending. Alpha at a pixel is opacity times the Gaussian's falloff $G$ at that pixel, so the same Gaussian contributes strongly at its center and almost nothing a few standard deviations away.

courseTitle: The ABA problem and tagged pointers
lessonTitle: LL/SC: watching the location instead of its value
md: LL/SC detects *writes*, so it is immune to A to B to A in principle. In practice the pop needs a load between LL and SC, which hardware does not guarantee to support, and languages expose CAS anyway.

courseTitle: Ablation studies: what each pipeline stage really adds
lessonTitle: Interaction effects and Shapley values
md: If two stages interact, no single number per stage tells the whole story. Test the key combinations (a 2 x 2 grid for a suspected pair), and when you need a per-stage split of the total, use Shapley values, which sum exactly to the full-minus-baseline gain.

courseTitle: Agent harnesses: the loop, tools, context and control around an LLM
lessonTitle: From one model call to an agent loop
md: A harness is a loop: call the model, run the tool calls it asks for, append the results, repeat until the model returns no tool calls or a budget runs out. Everything else (context management, permissions, traces, evals) is infrastructure around that loop.

courseTitle: Agent long-term memory: what to store, update, retrieve and forget
lessonTitle: The write path: extract facts, dedupe and resolve conflicts
md: Misconception: conflict resolution is a database problem you can solve with "latest write wins". Whether two facts conflict is a judgment about meaning ("eats fish" vs "vegetarian" share no words), which is why Mem0 asks an LLM. That also means the resolver can be wrong: a sarcastic "oh sure, I love meetings" can delete a real preference.

courseTitle: Agent verification: checking an agent's work before you trust it
lessonTitle: When more samples hurt, and how agreement helps
md: Misconception: more samples are always at least as good. Searching harder against a learned or LLM verifier is optimization against an imperfect proxy, which is reward hacking at inference time. Cap $N$ where measured accuracy peaks, not where your budget ends.

courseTitle: AI for materials discovery: stability, GNoME and MatterGen
lessonTitle: Cheap surrogates for DFT: graph networks and interatomic potentials
md: Judge a discovery surrogate by what it does to DFT spending: precision (hit rate), recall, and DAF on unrelaxed inputs. A low regression error does not guarantee good decisions near the hull.

courseTitle: Watermarking AI outputs
lessonTitle: Detection is a z-test on the green count
md: The normal approximation is optimistic for short texts. For $T = 50$, $\gamma = 0.25$ and 25 green tokens, $z = 4.08$ and the normal tail is $2.2 \times 10^{-5}$, but the exact binomial tail is $1.2 \times 10^{-4}$, about 5.5 times larger. Use the exact binomial when T is small.

courseTitle: Anomaly and outlier detection
lessonTitle: Why the mean and standard deviation hide outliers
md: Masking is the main failure of mean-based scores: several outliers inflate the standard deviation and hide one another. The NIST handbook also warns that applying a single-outlier test repeatedly does not fix this, because the first test may already report nothing.

courseTitle: Anomaly and outlier detection
lessonTitle: Evaluating detectors when 1 percent of points are anomalies
md: Do not report accuracy for anomaly detection: labeling everything normal scores 99 percent accuracy here. Be wary of ROC-AUC alone too. Report AP or a PR curve, plus precision@k at the review budget you actually have.

courseTitle: Asymmetric embeddings: query vs document input types
lessonTitle: Why a question is not a short version of its answer
md: Misconception: *a text's embedding is a fixed property of the text.* In a role-aware model the same string gets one vector as a query and a different vector as a document, by design. Which vector you get depends on how you called the model.

courseTitle: Calling LLM APIs at scale: concurrency, rate limits, retries, caching
lessonTitle: Rate limits as token buckets: RPM, token limits and headers
md: Do not cache or replay a 429 as if it were an answer. RFC 6585 says responses with status 429 "MUST NOT be stored by a cache". Also note that a 429 is not always temporary: Anthropic returns 429 without a `retry-after` header when an organization reaches its monthly spend cap, and retrying keeps failing until access resumes.

courseTitle: Async runtimes (Tokio) and coroutines
lessonTitle: Cooperative scheduling: blocking, budgets and cancellation
md: Async Rust in one breath: `async fn` compiles to a lazy state machine; `poll` advances it until an await is Pending; the waker plus the epoll-based driver decide when to poll again; Tokio's workers spread tasks with local queues and stealing; and because nothing preempts a task, every task must reach a Pending await often, or move blocking work to `spawn_blocking`.

courseTitle: Audio embeddings and classification
lessonTitle: Embeddings as features: VGGish, YAMNet and PANNs
md: Split by clip (or by source recording), never by patch. Patches of one clip overlap by 50% and share the same label, so a random patch-level split puts near-copies in train and test and inflates accuracy. ESC-50 ships 5 folds for this reason, and the TensorFlow tutorial carries each clip's fold number along with every patch embedding and splits by fold.

courseTitle: Autonomous research agents: plan, search, verify, evaluate
lessonTitle: End-to-end science agents: AI Scientist and co-scientist
md: End-to-end science agents fail at the steps where nothing external checks them: invented numbers, unfair comparisons, edits to their own limits. Put independent checks (sandboxes, reproducibility, human experts) at exactly those points.

courseTitle: Branch prediction and branchless code
lessonTitle: Why a pipelined CPU has to guess at every branch
md: A correctly predicted branch is nearly free. A mispredicted one costs about as many cycles as the pipeline is deep. Agner Fog gives roughly 0 to 2 cycles for a predicted branch and about 15 to 25 cycles for a misprediction on modern x86 cores.

courseTitle: B-trees vs LSM-trees and compaction
lessonTitle: B+trees update in place, and random writes pay for it
md: A B+tree's write cost is set by the **page**, not the row: a random small update rewrites a whole page at a random location. Reads are cheap because each key lives in exactly one place.

courseTitle: Buffer pools and page eviction: CLOCK, LRU-K and 2Q
lessonTitle: The buffer pool: frames, a page table, pins and dirty pages
md: A buffer pool is a write-back page cache owned by the database. On a miss it must evict some *unpinned* page, and write it out first if it is *dirty*. Everything else in this course is about choosing that page well.

courseTitle: Tokenizer-free and byte-level models
lessonTitle: Entropy patching: spend compute where the next byte is hard
md: Entropy depends on context, which can backfire. On a few-shot MMLU prompt, repeated phrases became very predictable, so they were swallowed into huge patches (the paper calls this entropy drift). The fix for the large run: reset the entropy model's context at newlines and use the monotonic rule.

courseTitle: C and Rust: from malloc and free to ownership and unsafe
lessonTitle: unsafe: five extra powers, same borrow checker
md: `unsafe` does not change the rules; it changes who checks them. Rust programs must never cause undefined behavior, inside or outside unsafe blocks. Inside, the proof obligation moves from the compiler to you.

courseTitle: Cache hierarchy (L1/L2/L3) and cache lines
lessonTitle: Where a line may live: sets, ways and tags
md: Power-of-two strides are a trap. In this L1d every address 4096 bytes apart maps to the same set, and a set has only 8 ways. Walking a column of `double m[N][512]` (rows of exactly 4 KB) puts every line in one set: only 8 of them can be cached at once even though the cache holds 512 lines.

courseTitle: Circuit tracing and attribution graphs
lessonTitle: Validating a graph with interventions
md: Graph first, intervention second. The graph proposes which features matter and how; perturbing those features in the real model is what turns a picture into evidence. Expect directional agreement, not exact numbers.

courseTitle: Click models and unbiased learning to rank
lessonTitle: Estimating propensities: swaps, EM, harvesting, dual learning
md: Pick the propensity source by how much user disruption you can afford: randomization or swaps are simplest and most trustworthy, EM and intervention harvesting use existing logs but rest on model assumptions, and DLA learns everything jointly. Every option inherits the click model's assumptions; if users behave like a cascade, a position-only propensity is misspecified.

courseTitle: Clustering: k-means, DBSCAN and finding failure patterns
lessonTitle: Choosing k: elbow, silhouette and their limits
md: Three things the silhouette cannot do. It is undefined for k = 1, so it can never tell you "this data has no clusters" (our k = 3 winner at 0.54 is not strong evidence of anything). It needs all pairwise distances, so it costs O(n squared) work. And it rewards compact well-separated blobs, so it is biased toward the kind of answer k-means produces, which makes it a poor referee between k-means and a density method.

courseTitle: Columnar storage and vectorized execution
lessonTitle: Inside a vectorized pipeline: primitives and selection vectors
md: A selection vector is not a filtered copy. Downstream primitives read the original vectors at the listed positions. That avoids copying, but the reads are now indirect and sparse, which matters for SIMD (next lesson).

courseTitle: Compilers and optimization levels (-O2, LTO, inlining)
lessonTitle: LTO and ThinLTO: optimizing across source files
md: LTO can expose latent bugs. Code with undefined behavior, or with mismatched declarations of the same function in different files, may have "worked" only because the optimizer could not see across files. When LTO breaks a program, suspect the program first.

courseTitle: Computer-use agents: seeing screens and driving mouse and keyboard
lessonTitle: Why long tasks fail: compounding errors and verification
md: Task success is roughly a product of step successes, so long tasks need both a high per-step rate and a check after each step that actually detects failure. Check the resulting state, not just whether an action ran.

courseTitle: Concurrency testing with loom and ThreadSanitizer
lessonTitle: ThreadSanitizer: catching races with vector clocks at runtime
md: TSan reports races that **did not cause a failure** in this run. It needs only that both conflicting accesses execute and that nothing orders them by happens-before. That is its big advantage over stress testing.

courseTitle: Consistency models: from linearizable to eventual
lessonTitle: What a consistency model promises, and why replicas break it
md: Model A is **stronger** than model B when every history A allows is also allowed by B (A is a subset of B). Stronger models rule out more surprising results, and usually cost more coordination, latency or availability.

courseTitle: Consistent hashing and hot-key mitigation
lessonTitle: The hash ring: each key goes to the next node clockwise
md: Consistent hashing minimises *movement*. It does not by itself give *balance*. With one random token per node, arcs vary wildly in size, as the toy ring shows. The next lesson fixes that.

courseTitle: Constraint satisfaction: hard filters, then soft scoring
lessonTitle: Too few results: relaxation ladders and post-hoc constraints
md: Three layers, three tools: per-document requirements are **filters**, per-document preferences are a **weighted score**, and requirements on the list as a whole are a **re-ranking pass**. When filters starve the list, relax in a declared order, keep the non-negotiables hard, and say what you relaxed.

courseTitle: Constraint satisfaction solvers: backtracking, AC-3, CDCL and CP-SAT
lessonTitle: CP-SAT in practice: lazy clauses, models and statuses
md: A solver turns a declarative model into search plus propagation plus learning. Your job is the model: tight domains, global constraints instead of many small ones, integer scaling, and a time limit with a status check.

courseTitle: Conversational query refinement: tracking search state across turns
lessonTitle: Resolving the second one and those against what was shown
md: Do not ask the LLM to copy job ids out of text. Give it the shown list with positions and attributes and let it output a position or an attribute match; code does the lookup. A model that types ids can produce a well-formed id that was never shown.

courseTitle: Chain-of-thought faithfulness and monitorability
lessonTitle: Do reasoning models admit the hints they use?
md: When the model can act on information without reasoning about it, its CoT usually stays silent about it, even with no pressure to hide. CoT monitoring then helps you notice frequent behaviors, but it cannot certify that a behavior is absent.

courseTitle: Cross-encoder rerankers: scoring query and document together
lessonTitle: Why a reranker reads the query and the document together
md: A cross-encoder is not a better embedding model. It has no vector output you could store in a vector database. If someone asks you to index a corpus with a reranker, the answer is that you cannot: the score exists only for a specific query.

courseTitle: CUTLASS and CuTe: tiling GEMMs across the GPU memory hierarchy
lessonTitle: Why a fast GEMM is a hierarchy of tiles
md: Intensity per tile is not the whole story. Two CTAs that share a row of tiles both read the same slice of A, and the L2 cache may serve the second read. CUTLASS's threadblock rasterization (swizzling the CTA launch order) exists to make that L2 reuse more likely.

courseTitle: CUTLASS and CuTe: tiling GEMMs across the GPU memory hierarchy
lessonTitle: The CUTLASS 3.x API, epilogues and tuning tradeoffs
md: Fast CUTLASS kernels come from a few choices: tile shape (reuse versus occupancy and wave fit), stage count (latency hiding versus shared memory), kernel schedule (cooperative or ping-pong) and the epilogue fusion. CuTe layouts make each choice a type parameter instead of a rewrite.

courseTitle: CXL and memory disaggregation: far memory you can load and store
lessonTitle: Placing pages: tiering in Linux, pooling in Pond
md: CXL makes memory placement a policy problem again. The hardware gives you a slower, bigger NUMA tier; the operating system (tiering) or the cluster manager (pooling) must keep hot data local and push only cold or untouched data to it.

courseTitle: Data-oriented design: struct-of-arrays vs array-of-structs
lessonTitle: Why a loop over objects wastes most of each cache line
md: SoA is not automatically faster. Its advantage is exactly the fraction of each record that a loop does *not* touch. A loop that uses every field gains nothing from the layout change, and some access patterns get worse (lesson 2).

courseTitle: Deterministic inference: bitwise equivalence and reproducibility
lessonTitle: Two orderings, two answers: float addition is not associative
md: Floating-point addition is commutative but not associative. Reordering a sum is not a refactor, it is a different computation. Every other idea in this course follows from that sentence.

courseTitle: Diffusion language models: generating text by unmasking
lessonTitle: Why generate text in any order other than left to right?
md: A diffusion language model keeps the Transformer and the maximum-likelihood goal of a GPT. It changes two things: attention is bidirectional, and generation fills in many masked positions per step in any order instead of one token at the end.

courseTitle: Disaggregated prefill and decode
lessonTitle: Why prefill stalls decode on a shared GPU
md: Prefill is compute-bound and sets TTFT; decode is memory-bound and sets TPOT. Putting both in one batch makes each phase pay for the other.

courseTitle: DiskANN and CAGRA: billion-scale ANN on SSDs and GPUs
lessonTitle: Vamana: RobustPrune and the alpha knob
md: A common misreading: larger alpha prunes *more*. It is the opposite. The removal test gets harder to pass as alpha grows, so more candidates survive, the average degree rises (up to the cap R), and search paths get shorter. The cost is memory and more distance computations per hop.

courseTitle: DPO and its variants: preference tuning without RL
lessonTitle: KTO: aligning with thumbs up and thumbs down, no pairs
md: KTO keeps DPO's implicit reward and reference model but drops pairing: each example is scored against a shared reference point (the estimated KL drift) instead of against a sibling answer. That lets it train on binary feedback, and on imbalanced data via $\lambda_D, \lambda_U$.

courseTitle: Online data migration (dual-write and backfill)
lessonTitle: Proving the new read path before trusting it
md: Scientist is for code that only reads. Its README says that because the candidate may or may not run, it is only safe for wrapping methods that do not change data. Write paths need different checks, such as comparing stored rows after the fact.

courseTitle: eBPF tracing with bpftrace: probes, verifier, maps
lessonTitle: The verifier: proving every path safe before it runs
md: The verifier runs once, at load time, and proves properties of **all** paths: bounded execution, typed pointers, null checks before dereference, initialized registers, in-bounds stack and map access. Because the proof is done up front, the JIT-compiled code needs no runtime checks and runs at native speed.

courseTitle: Efficient reasoning: overthinking and length control
lessonTitle: Measuring wasted tokens and training them away
md: Plain SFT on short samples barely helped here (a 2.0% cut on MATH500). Imitating short traces is weaker than contrasting short against long, because the model never sees what it should move away from.

courseTitle: Energy disaggregation (NILM): from Hart's edges to seq2point
lessonTitle: One meter, many appliances: the disaggregation problem
md: NILM is an inverse problem: one observed sum, many hidden parts. Every algorithm you will meet differs only in what extra knowledge it uses to choose among the many decompositions that add up to the same total.

courseTitle: Entity normalization: job titles, schools and companies
lessonTitle: Blocking: compare only pairs that could match
md: A pair that blocking drops is classified as a non-match without ever being looked at. No scoring model can recover it. Use several strict rules joined by OR (Splink's advice: a longer list of strict rules beats a short list of loose ones), so a typo in one field is caught by a rule on another.

courseTitle: epoll and event loops: serving many sockets from one thread
lessonTitle: Inside epoll: interest list, ready list, epoll_wait
md: epoll cannot help with disk files. `epoll_ctl` fails with `EPERM` for a regular file or directory, and poll reports such files as always ready, because a disk read never becomes "ready" in advance: it just has to wait for the device. Event loops send file I/O to a thread pool (next lessons) or use io_uring.

courseTitle: Avoiding overfitting to a public query set
lessonTitle: Split by query and keep a rotating sealed test set
md: Hold out queries, not pairs, and cluster near-duplicates before splitting. Tune on dev as much as you like, read the sealed test set rarely and for decisions you declared in advance, and replace it on a schedule.

courseTitle: False sharing and cache-line padding
lessonTitle: Why a write steals the whole line: MESI and ownership
md: False sharing needs three things at once: two or more cores, one cache line, and at least one writer. Remove any one (single thread, separate lines, or read-only data) and the line stops bouncing.

courseTitle: Federated learning: training without moving the data
lessonTitle: Non-IID data and client drift: fast convergence to the wrong answer
md: Simplified model: ours is one parameter, convex, deterministic, full-batch and fully participating. Real drift in a deep network is worse and messier (it interacts with batch normalization statistics, momentum and client sampling), but the direction of the error is the one computed here.

courseTitle: Fine-grained MoE, shared experts, aux-loss-free load balancing
lessonTitle: From one MLP to many routed experts
md: Separate two numbers for every MoE model: **total parameters** (all experts, what you store) and **activated parameters** (what one token actually uses, which sets FLOPs per token). DeepSeek-V3 has 671B total and 37B activated per token.

courseTitle: FlashAttention-3 and FlashAttention-4
lessonTitle: FlashAttention-4 backward, scheduling, and using the kernels
md: Each generation chases the bottleneck the previous hardware exposed. FlashAttention removed HBM traffic for $S$ and $P$. FlashAttention-2 fixed work partitioning. FlashAttention-3 used Hopper's asynchrony to hide softmax and loads under the matmuls. FlashAttention-4 attacks the exponential unit and shared memory bandwidth, which stopped scaling with Blackwell's tensor cores.

courseTitle: Flow matching and rectified flow
lessonTitle: Crossing lines and why the learned paths curve
md: Straight training targets do not mean straight sampling paths. Each conditional path is a line, but the marginal flow, which is what the network learns and what sampling follows, curves wherever many lines cross.

courseTitle: FP8 and FP4 training: E4M3, scaling, MXFP4 and NVFP4
lessonTitle: What 8 and 4 bits can hold: E4M3, E5M2 and E2M1
md: "FP8 training" does not mean every tensor is FP8. In the FP8 paper, DeepSeek-V3 and the NVFP4 report alike, only the *inputs* to GEMMs are FP8. GEMM outputs come out in BF16 or FP32, and normalizations, softmax, the master weights and optimizer state stay in higher precision.

courseTitle: fsync, write-ahead logs and group commit
lessonTitle: The write-ahead rule: flush the log first, pages later
md: The write-ahead rule, in PostgreSQL's words: changes to data files must be written only after the log records describing them have been flushed to permanent storage. A commit is durable once its commit record is flushed; data pages can be written much later.

courseTitle: Fuzzy matching and string similarity
lessonTitle: Indexes that skip most strings: trigram filters and BK-trees
md: Both indexes trade exactness of the first step for speed: a trigram index proposes candidates by a cheap overlap count, a BK-tree rules out subtrees with the triangle inequality. Neither changes the final score; you still verify candidates with the metric you trust.

courseTitle: Geometric hashing and star-pattern plate solving
lessonTitle: Verification: accepting a match only when the odds reach a billion
md: Retrieval is cheap and noisy; verification is strict. Each match is a full alignment that predicts many other stars, and the Bayes factor multiplies independent evidence, so a true match passes 1e9 within a handful of stars while chance matches almost never do.

courseTitle: GPU image operators: resize, warp, color convert and convolution
lessonTitle: Pixels in memory: NHWC, NCHW, pitch and a warp's 96 bytes
md: For a per-pixel operator, layout plus pitch decides how wide an aligned access each lane can make. NHWC gives a pixel's channels locality and lets one load carry a whole pixel when channels are padded to 4; NCHW gives each channel a unit-stride stream. Neither is wrong, and both lose if the kernel accesses one byte at a time.

courseTitle: GPU memory allocators and suballocation
lessonTitle: Best fit, splitting and merging inside segments
md: Best fit plus split plus merge keeps reuse high, but a free hole only helps if it is big enough. Watch the gap between total free and the largest free block, not just the totals.

courseTitle: GPU memory hierarchy and coalescing
lessonTitle: How a warp's 32 addresses become 32-byte sectors
md: Count distinct 32-byte sectors per warp request. 4 for 32 consecutive floats is ideal; 32 is the worst case and wastes 87.5% of the traffic.

courseTitle: GPU profiling and speed-of-light analysis with Nsight
lessonTitle: Reading the Speed Of Light rows
md: Speed Of Light does not tell you what to fix. It tells you which of four investigations to open, and whether the kernel has any headroom at all.

courseTitle: CUDA and Metal programming model: threads, blocks, warps
lessonTitle: Cooperating inside a block: shared memory, barriers and clusters
md: `__syncthreads()` may appear in conditional code only if the condition evaluates the same way for every thread in the block. Otherwise execution may hang or produce unintended side effects. Hoist the barrier out of the branch.

courseTitle: GraphRAG: entity graphs, communities, and global search
lessonTitle: Community summaries and map-reduce global search
md: Global search is not cheap per query. The docs call it resource-intensive: the map step makes one LLM call per batch of reports, so lower (more detailed) levels cost more calls. Picking the community level is a quality versus cost dial.

courseTitle: GRPO and RLVR: RL with verifiable rewards
lessonTitle: Why PPO is costly for LLMs and what GRPO removes
md: GRPO removes the **critic**, not the reward. In DeepSeekMath, GRPO was trained against a learned reward model. Rule-based verifiable rewards came to the fore with DeepSeek-R1. GRPO and RLVR are separate ideas that work well together.

courseTitle: Transit feeds: GTFS Schedule and GTFS Realtime
lessonTitle: Joining realtime to the schedule and propagating delay
md: Do not propagate across trips by default. A bus 15 minutes late on T1 may or may not start its next trip late, depending on the layover. The spec encourages producers to publish TripUpdates for the next trips the same vehicle will run (its block, from block_id in trips.txt) when they are confident, precisely so consumers do not have to guess.

courseTitle: Huge pages: 2 MiB and 1 GiB mappings, hugetlbfs and THP
lessonTitle: What 4 KiB pages cost a 16 GiB working set
md: These are load counts, not latencies. CPUs keep paging-structure caches and multiple TLB levels with model-specific sizes, so a real miss usually skips some loads. The ratios show the direction of the effect; only a measurement on your hardware gives the size.

courseTitle: Hybrid attention and SSM models
lessonTitle: Why a fixed-size state forgets and a KV cache does not
md: The hybrid bet: SSM or linear-attention layers do most of the sequence mixing cheaply, and a handful of full attention layers act as an exact lookup into the past. The Mamba-2 authors put it as SSM layers being a general sequence-to-sequence map while attention layers are "a retrieval mechanism to quickly refer to previous tokens".

courseTitle: Hybrid search: fusing BM25 and dense retrieval
lessonTitle: A cross-encoder reranks the fused shortlist
md: Fusion is about **recall of the shortlist**; reranking is about **precision at the top**. Fused-list quality caps what the reranker can achieve, and rerank depth N trades latency for the chance to rescue documents fused low.

courseTitle: Image alignment (homography) and change detection
lessonTitle: Differencing and picking a threshold with Otsu's method
md: Otsu always returns a threshold, even when nothing changed. On a pair with pure noise it will happily split the noise into two classes and flag a large fraction of the image. Check for a clear gap (or a minimum difference between class means) before trusting the mask.

courseTitle: io_uring: asynchronous I/O through shared rings
lessonTitle: Links, drains, timeouts and a CQ that never overflows
md: Size the **CQ** for the maximum number of completions that can be outstanding (including several per request for multishot operations), not the SQ. Use `IORING_SETUP_CQSIZE` with `cq_entries`, and reap promptly.

courseTitle: jemalloc, mimalloc and tcmalloc internals
lessonTitle: Cross-thread frees, idle caches and returning memory
md: Choose by the hard constraint. Many threads and a tight memory budget favour per-CPU caching (tcmalloc). Heavy cross-thread freeing and allocation-heavy runtimes suit mimalloc's per-page lists. Fine-grained control over arenas, decay and introspection (`mallctl`, stats) is jemalloc's strength. Then tune the return-to-OS delay against page-fault cost.

courseTitle: Kernel autotuning and configuration search
lessonTitle: Why the winner changes when the shape changes
md: A configuration is only ever best **for a shape on a device**. That is why the tuning result has to be stored under a key that contains the shape, and why `triton.autotune` takes `key=['M', 'N', 'K']`: the docs say a change in those values triggers evaluation of all provided configs.

courseTitle: Kernel bypass: driving NICs and NVMe from user space (DPDK, SPDK)
lessonTitle: Scaling across cores: one queue per core, rings and mempools
md: Scaling rule for bypass stacks: **one queue, one owner**. Hardware queues give each core a private path to the device, mempool caches give it private buffers, and rings or messages are the only places cores meet, always in bursts.

courseTitle: Kernel fusion: moving fewer bytes through HBM
lessonTitle: Limits of fusion and how compilers decide
md: A fusion is worth it when it removes HBM round trips or launches without blowing the on-chip budget or recomputing expensive work. Compilers estimate bytes saved, check legality, and fuse greedily; in training they also choose between saving and recomputing activations.

courseTitle: Knowledge distillation: teaching a small model with a big one
lessonTitle: When distillation works, when it fails, and what it costs
md: Distillation trades extra training compute (running a teacher) for a cheaper model to serve. It works best when the student can realistically imitate the teacher; when the gap is large, shrink it with an assistant or an easier teacher.

courseTitle: KV cache compression and quantization
lessonTitle: Beyond rounding: pre-RoPE keys, outliers, and FP8 in production
md: FP8 without calibration uses a scale of 1.0. That works when values fit FP8's range, but calibrated scales are what vLLM recommends for best accuracy, and some layers (such as sliding-window ones) can be kept in the native dtype.

courseTitle: KV cache offloading: tiers, reload vs recompute, and eviction
lessonTitle: Hiding the transfer: layer-wise loading and asynchronous saving
md: Overlap turns load plus compute into roughly max(load, compute). It is free speed when the two are balanced and nearly useless when one dominates.

courseTitle: Clocks: Lamport, vector and hybrid logical clocks
lessonTitle: Vector clocks: detecting concurrency exactly
md: Lamport clocks give one-way causality in one integer. Vector clocks give exact causality and detect concurrency, at the cost of one integer per node in every timestamp and every message.

courseTitle: Late interaction: ColBERT, PLAID and ColPali
lessonTitle: Searching millions of passages: candidates, centroids, PLAID
md: Cheap approximate scores filter, exact scores decide. PLAID is the same funnel as BM25 followed by a cross-encoder, built inside one model: centroid ids are the cheap representation and decompressed vectors are the precise one.

courseTitle: Latent reasoning: chain of continuous thought (Coconut)
lessonTitle: Latent search: one thought, several frontier nodes
md: BFS-like (breadth-first-search-like) is an interpretation from probing, not a built-in algorithm. Coconut was never trained to search, keeps no explicit visited set, and the parallelism narrows after a couple of thoughts.

courseTitle: Learned indexes: replacing B-tree search with a fitted model
lessonTitle: Error windows, exponential search and monotonic models
md: Always handle the case where the search lands on the edge of the window. With stored min/max bounds, a hit on the boundary is the signal that a non-monotonic model may have pushed the true answer outside.

courseTitle: Learned sparse retrieval with SPLADE
lessonTitle: SPLADE v2, SPLADE++ and running it in production
md: Do not read the tokens as an explanation. Elastic's docs warn that expansion terms are learned associations, not synonyms, and that low-weight tokens carry information jointly, much like dimensions of a dense vector. A surprising token in a result is not by itself a bug.

courseTitle: Linear attention and Gated DeltaNet
lessonTitle: Dropping the softmax turns attention into an RNN
md: Linear attention is one function with two schedules: a **parallel form** $O=(QK^\top\odot M)V$ that is matmul-friendly for training, and a **recurrent form** $S_t=S_{t-1}+v_tk_t^\top$, $o_t=S_tq_t$ with constant time and memory per generated token.

courseTitle: LLM-as-judge for relevance labeling
lessonTitle: Measuring judge agreement: confusion matrix and Cohen's kappa
md: Always say which agreement number you report. UMBRELA's GPT-4o labels on TREC DL 2019 to 2023 had 4-grade kappa 0.31 to 0.37 but binarised kappa 0.42 to 0.50 on the same labels. A paper quoting one and a dashboard quoting the other are not comparable.

courseTitle: LLM inference systems and KV-cache memory management
lessonTitle: KV cache accounting: from bytes per token to batch size
md: Capacity in sequences is roughly pool bytes / (bytes per token x tokens per sequence). Every lever (GQA, FP8 KV, more GPUs, smaller weights, shorter contexts, less waste per sequence) moves one of those three terms.

courseTitle: LLM prompting and structured output: from prompts to masked logits
lessonTitle: Why asking nicely for JSON is not enough
md: Three different promises are easy to confuse: *parses as JSON*, *matches my schema*, and *is correct*. JSON mode gives the first, schema-constrained output gives the second, and only your own validation and evaluation can check the third.

courseTitle: LLM query parsing: natural language to structured filters
lessonTitle: Evaluating the parser with exact match per field
md: The predictions in this lesson are hand-written to show typical error types. They are not measurements of any model. Use the method, not the numbers.

courseTitle: Latency and cost tradeoffs for LLM reranking
lessonTitle: Prefix caching, truncation and smaller candidate lists
md: Every input saving has a quality price. Truncation can cut the sentence that made a passage relevant. A smaller $k$ means relevant documents retrieved at rank 31 or lower are never reranked. Measure NDCG@10 at each setting on your own queries before shipping the cheaper one.

courseTitle: Local feature matching: Harris, SIFT, ORB and RANSAC
lessonTitle: Why corners make good features: the Harris response
md: Harris is invariant to rotation (eigenvalues do not change when the image rotates) but **not to scale**. Zoom in on a corner enough and, inside a fixed 3x3 window, it looks like an edge. Lesson 2 fixes this.

courseTitle: Lock-free stacks and queues: Treiber, Michael-Scott, Vyukov
lessonTitle: Why a preempted lock holder stalls everyone
md: "No mutex in the code" does not make an algorithm lock-free. If one stalled thread can prevent all others from completing, it is blocking, even if it only uses atomic instructions. Michael and Scott call out published queues that are "lock-free but not non-blocking" for exactly this reason, and Vyukov says the same of their own bounded queue (lesson 5).

courseTitle: Lock-free stacks and queues: Treiber, Michael-Scott, Vyukov
lessonTitle: Freeing nodes safely: hazard pointers and epochs
md: Lock-free data structures are two problems: the CAS protocol that keeps the structure consistent, and the reclamation scheme that keeps removed nodes alive until no thread can still be reading them. Get both right, or use a library that has.

courseTitle: Long context: RoPE scaling, YaRN and Ring Attention
lessonTitle: Why models break past their trained length
md: RoPE is called a relative encoding, so it is tempting to think it should extrapolate for free. It does not: dimensions whose wavelength exceeds the training length never wrap, so in practice they leak absolute position, and new positions mean new, unseen angles.

courseTitle: Long context: RoPE scaling, YaRN and Ring Attention
lessonTitle: Hiding communication, causal balance and Ulysses
md: Overlap condition: $c \ge F/B$. Fast links (NVLink, TPU ICI) need blocks of about 1K tokens; slow links need tens of thousands. Causal masks require striping or zigzag chunk assignment, or the busiest rank sets the pace.

courseTitle: Looped and recurrent-depth transformers
lessonTitle: Spending compute at test time: more loops, early exits, shared caches
md: Per-token early exit saves FLOPs per token, but in batched serving tokens that exit early may sit idle waiting for others. Relaxed Recursive Transformers (Bae et al. 2024) propose **continuous depth-wise batching**, scheduling new work into slots freed by early exits; their simulation estimates 2 to 3x throughput, not a measured deployment.

courseTitle: Machine unlearning: removing data and knowledge from trained models
lessonTitle: Hidden, not gone: relearning, probing and quantization attacks
md: A model that passes forget-set benchmarks in full precision can fail them after an ordinary 4-bit conversion that a user applies for deployment. Any release that relies on unlearning should evaluate the quantized versions people will actually run.

courseTitle: Megatron-Core performance: TP, PP, SP, CP and MFU
lessonTitle: Why one GPU cannot train a 175B model, and the five ways to split it
md: Every axis splits something different: TP splits matrices, PP splits layers, DP splits the batch, CP splits the sequence, EP splits experts. Choosing a configuration means choosing which communication you can afford on which link.

courseTitle: Memory fragmentation: why freed memory stays used
lessonTitle: Free memory you cannot use: two kinds of fragmentation
md: Internal fragmentation is waste inside handed-out blocks (a rounding cost). External fragmentation is free memory split into holes too small to use (a placement and lifetime cost). Both are measured against live data, and the number depends on when you measure.

courseTitle: Memory ordering (acquire/release, seq_cst) and the C++/Rust model
lessonTitle: Relaxed: one agreed history per variable, nothing more
md: Myth: "Relaxed writes may take ages to show up, and SeqCst makes them visible sooner." The memory model says nothing about timing at all, only about order. A stronger ordering does not make data travel faster; it may even slow your program down.

courseTitle: Memory reclamation: epochs, hazard pointers, RCU
lessonTitle: Epoch-based reclamation: free garbage two epochs later
md: Holding a guard is holding back everyone's garbage. Pinning across a blocking call, a lock wait or a long iteration stops the epoch from advancing for all threads. crossbeam provides `Guard::repin` to briefly unpin and pin again inside long loops; references loaded before the repin are no longer protected.

courseTitle: Metric learning and re-identification
lessonTitle: Triplet loss: the margin and easy, semi-hard, hard negatives
md: Hard is not the same as useful. The very hardest negatives in a large dataset are often mislabeled or badly imaged examples (FaceNet names both). Training only on them teaches the network to fit noise.

courseTitle: Microbenchmarking pitfalls: when the number lies
lessonTitle: Warm caches in the benchmark, cold caches in production
md: Misconception: "warm-up makes a benchmark more accurate". It makes it measure **steady state**. If your function really runs once per request on cold caches, the warmed number is precise and wrong. Decide which regime production is in, then measure that one.

courseTitle: Miles: production RL post-training forked from slime
lessonTitle: Fully async RL: busy engines, paid for in staleness
md: Fully async makes training **off-policy**: the trainer learns from groups generated under older weights. The docs recommend staying synchronous while you debug a recipe or validate loss and reward code, where an exact on-policy cadence matters more than throughput.

courseTitle: ML for systems: learned indexes, caching and scheduling
lessonTitle: Why hand-tuned policies leave a gap: LRU versus Belady's MIN
md: In all three systems the model chooses among **correct** options: any position inside a verified error window, any cached object to evict, any runnable stage to schedule. A bad model can make the system slower, but the surrounding structure keeps it correct.

courseTitle: Multi-head latent attention (MLA)
lessonTitle: Absorbing the up-projections: attend in latent space
md: Absorption is just regrouping a product of matrices: $q^{\top}(W c) = (W^{\top} q)^{\top} c$. It turns MLA decoding into MQA-shaped work over the latent cache, so no per-head key or value is ever stored or rebuilt.

courseTitle: Multi-query retrieval: many phrasings, one fused result
lessonTitle: Drift, redundancy, reranker budgets, and when to skip it
md: Asking for diversity cuts both ways. Raudaschl's repo has a diverse mode whose prompt asks for synonyms, broader or narrower framings and related sub-topics, and to avoid minor rewordings. That reduces redundancy but pushes phrasings toward the edge of the topic, where drift lives. Inspect generated queries on real traffic before tuning N.

courseTitle: Multi-token prediction: training GPTs to look ahead
lessonTitle: From one target per position to n targets per position
md: Multi-token prediction keeps the input and the causal context the same and only adds targets: each position is asked for tokens t+1 through t+n, all from the prefix ending at t.

courseTitle: Muon, Shampoo and SOAP: optimizers that treat weights as matrices
lessonTitle: Muon: orthogonalize the momentum with a few matrix multiplies
md: Muon does not produce an exactly orthogonal matrix. The reference implementation's docstring says the result is closer to $US'V^\top$ with the entries of $S'$ roughly uniform in $[0.5, 1.5]$, and that this does not hurt model performance. The Moonlight team also found 10 steps gave a more accurate result than 5 but no better training.

courseTitle: muP: tune a small model, transfer hyperparameters to a large one
lessonTitle: What breaks in SP after a single training step
md: Random weights times activations grow like sqrt(n); updates times activations grow like n, because updates are correlated with the activations they act on. muP sets each layer's init and learning rate so that both effects stay order 1.

courseTitle: Mutexes, spinlocks and futexes: how locks really wait
lessonTitle: The futex: sleep on an address, wake by address
md: Returning from FUTEX_WAIT does not mean the lock is yours. The call can fail with EAGAIN, be interrupted by a signal (EINTR), or wake spuriously, and another thread may grab the lock first. Always loop and re-check the word.

courseTitle: MVCC and transaction isolation levels
lessonTitle: Read Committed vs Repeatable Read: when the snapshot is taken
md: Read Committed: new snapshot per statement, writers re-apply on top of concurrent commits. Repeatable Read: one snapshot per transaction, writers that hit a concurrent commit get error 40001 and must retry.

courseTitle: Named entity recognition: tagging spans in text
lessonTitle: The metric: entity-level micro F1 with exact span match
md: Never report token accuracy for NER. CoNLL-2003 English training data holds one entity per 8.7 tokens, so the great majority of tags are O and a tagger that predicts O everywhere scores high token accuracy with an entity F1 of exactly zero. Entity-level micro F1 is the metric; token accuracy is a training diagnostic at best.

courseTitle: Near-duplicate image search with perceptual hashes
lessonTitle: Why MD5 misses copies, and the average hash that does not
md: A perceptual hash is a summary you **compare**, not an identity you **look up**. Similar images give hashes at a small Hamming distance; the system decides a threshold for what counts as a match.

courseTitle: NeMo RL: NVIDIA's Ray-based post-training library
lessonTitle: Training backends (Automodel, Megatron) and generation backends
md: Training parallelism and generation parallelism are separate settings. For example vLLM's `tensor_parallel_size` is unrelated to Megatron's `tensor_model_parallel_size`. Refit must reshape weights from the trainer's layout into the engine's layout, which is part of why refit transports matter (lesson 4).

courseTitle: NUMA: placing memory and threads on multi-socket machines
lessonTitle: Memory policies: local, bind, preferred and interleave
md: Policy = mode + nodes + scope, applied at allocation time. Use bind for strict isolation, preferred when spilling over is acceptable, interleave for big shared data, and leave private per-thread data on the default local policy.

courseTitle: Object detection and counting
lessonTitle: What a detector outputs, and how two boxes are compared
md: A detector outputs a variable-size set of (box, class, score) triples, and IoU between boxes is the measure every later stage builds on.

courseTitle: Object detection and counting
lessonTitle: Counting objects: by detection, by density, by tracking
md: Pick the counting method by scene: detection when objects are separable and you need locations, density maps for dense crowds where boxes fail, and tracking plus line or region events for video, where the same object appears in many frames.

courseTitle: Observability: metrics, traces, dashboards and SLOs
lessonTitle: Counters, gauges, histograms, and the quantile you must not average
md: Never compute a rate as last value minus first value over a counter. One restart in the window turns a positive rate into a large negative number, and `rate()` exists precisely to handle that case for you.

courseTitle: OCR and document understanding: from pixels to fields
lessonTitle: Why OCR is a pipeline: find the text, then read it
md: OCR is a chain: detect, then recognize, then order and extract. Each stage only sees the previous stage's output, so an early error silently becomes a wrong field later.

courseTitle: Building large projects from source (CMake, CUDA builds)
lessonTitle: A build is a graph: why one edit rebuilds 4 files, not 1 or 500
md: Rebuild cost is decided by the include graph. Touching a header recompiles every translation unit that reaches it, directly or transitively. That is why big projects keep widely included headers small and stable.

courseTitle: CI pipelines and test suites: from red checks to reliable tests
lessonTitle: Jobs, needs and matrices: how one push becomes many runs
md: A red X on one matrix cell with grey cancelled cells next to it does not mean the other platforms passed. With fail-fast they never finished. Look at which job failed first; that is the one with the real log.

courseTitle: Code review: responding to and giving review
lessonTitle: Answering review comments as the author
md: Never reply in anger. Google's guide calls it a serious breach of etiquette that lives forever in the review tool. If a comment stings, ask what constructive point the reviewer is making, and answer that point once you are calm.

courseTitle: Contribution norms: CONTRIBUTING, issues, conduct and AI policies
lessonTitle: Issue first: when to ask, how to report, how to claim work
md: Closing keywords (`close`, `closes`, `closed`, `fix`, `fixes`, `fixed`, `resolve`, `resolves`, `resolved`) only work when the PR targets the repository's **default branch**. Aimed at a release or feature branch, the keyword is ignored and the issue stays open after merge.

courseTitle: Git workflow for pull requests: fork, branch, rebase, sign-off
lessonTitle: Keeping a branch current: rebase onto upstream/main
md: Rebasing replays your commits on a new base. Every replayed commit gets a new hash because its parent changed, even if its diff is identical.

courseTitle: Open source licenses, CLAs and the DCO
lessonTitle: No license means no permission: what a license grants
md: A license is permission plus conditions. The conditions only apply when you do the thing they attach to, which for most licenses means distributing the code.

courseTitle: Performance PRs: benchmark evidence and regression checks
lessonTitle: What a reviewer needs before merging a speedup
md: A performance claim is an experiment. The PR must let a reviewer rerun it (exact commands, setup, commits) and weigh it (spread, significance and costs), not just read a headline number.

courseTitle: Reading a large codebase: search, trace and dig through history
lessonTitle: Search that narrows: git grep, ripgrep and word matches
md: GitHub's "find references" is name-based: the docs say it searches all definitions and references across a repository "to find entities with a given name". Two unrelated functions with the same name in different modules will both show up. Check the file and its imports before you trust a reference.

courseTitle: Reproducing bugs: minimal repros, delta debugging and git bisect
lessonTitle: Delta debugging: let a script shrink the repro
md: Automated reduction needs only a yes or no oracle: does this candidate still show the exact failure? Write that test carefully and the tool does the tedious part.

courseTitle: Writing a reviewable pull request
lessonTitle: One logical change per PR, and every commit builds
md: Each PR (and each commit in a series) should be justifiable on its own and leave the project building and passing tests. If one depends on another, say so in the description.

courseTitle: PagedAttention and prefix caching
lessonTitle: Block tables: virtual memory for the KV cache
md: Paging is not free. The paper measured 20 to 26% higher attention kernel latency than FasterTransformer's kernel, from block-table lookups, extra branches and variable lengths. It still wins end to end because only the attention operator pays, and the larger batch more than makes up for it.

courseTitle: perf and flame graphs
lessonTitle: From perf.data to folded stacks
md: In `perf report`, a high Children value does not mean the function is doing the work. main is 100% in every program. Sort by Self to find what executes, by Children to find which caller to change.

courseTitle: Persistent memory data structures: crash consistency per cache line
lessonTitle: Why a finished store is not yet durable
md: Visibility and durability are different events. A store becomes visible when it reaches the coherent cache, and durable only when its line reaches the persistence domain. On ADR platforms, software must close that gap explicitly.

courseTitle: Pose estimation: heatmaps, grouping, OKS and joint angles
lessonTitle: What a pose model outputs and the top-down pipeline
md: A top-down pose model inherits every mistake of its detector. If two people overlap and NMS merges their boxes, or the detector misses someone, the keypoint network has no way to recover that person. OpenPose's authors call this **early commitment**.

courseTitle: Pre-filtering vs post-filtering with metadata
lessonTitle: Post-filtering: why top-k comes back short
md: Post-filtering leaves the index untouched and is cheap when $s$ is large, but the result count is a random variable. To hold k results you must fetch on the order of $k/s$ candidates, and noticeably more for a high-probability guarantee.

courseTitle: Prefetching, memory bandwidth versus latency
lessonTitle: Hardware prefetchers: patterns, training and the page wall
md: Hardware prefetching is not free: every useless prefetch costs memory bandwidth and can evict a line you still needed. That is how it can make a random walk slower than raw memory latency. Drepper describes Intel's model-specific register switch for disabling it (bit 9 of IA32_MISC_ENABLE on many processors of that time) for workloads that measurably suffer.

courseTitle: Process reward models: grading reasoning one step at a time
lessonTitle: Failure modes, evaluation, and why some labs skip PRMs
md: Do not judge a PRM only by best-of-N accuracy. That metric checks final answers, rewards PRMs that act like outcome models, and depends on which generator produced the samples. Check step-level error location (for example ProcessBench) on the distribution you will actually run it on.

courseTitle: Product quantization (PQ)
lessonTitle: Why billion-vector indexes need compressed codes
md: PQ builds an exponentially large codebook, $(k^*)^m$ centroids, out of $m$ tiny ones. Each vector costs $m \log_2 k^*$ bits no matter how many dimensions it has.

courseTitle: Protein design with diffusion over residue frames
lessonTitle: Sequence design, then the self-consistency check
md: Self-consistency grades a generator with a predictor that was trained on natural proteins, and both can be wrong in the same direction. A design that AF2 loves is not proven to fold: it has passed one cheap filter. Everything after this point costs money and weeks.

courseTitle: Query rewriting and decomposition
lessonTitle: Conversational rewriting: turning a follow-up into a standalone query
md: Misconception: the rewriter should make the query richer. Its job is to make it *standalone and faithful*. A rewriter that adds guessed facts (say, `when the leader fails during a network partition`) can steer retrieval toward documents the user never asked about. Instruct it not to answer, and to return the message unchanged when it is already standalone.

courseTitle: RaBitQ and binary quantization: 1-bit vectors with error bounds
lessonTitle: Computing the estimate with popcount, and re-ranking by the bound
md: Per vector, the query-time work is a few AND plus popcount passes over the D-bit code and a handful of multiply-adds with precomputed factors. The error bound then tells you which candidates are worth an exact distance.

courseTitle: Retrieval-augmented generation: the pipeline and its failures
lessonTitle: Indexing: how chunk size and overlap decide what can be found
md: Small chunks lose their context. D1.5 reads *or adoption. Send leave requests to the People team, who approve them.* It never says which leave. In a real handbook with ten leave policies it would match every leave question equally well. Bigger chunks keep context but dilute the embedding and spend more of the prompt.

courseTitle: Feature engineering for ranking
lessonTitle: Document, query and interaction signals: freshness, popularity, clicks
md: Shape raw signals before the model sees them: turn age into a decaying freshness, counts into logs or rates, and remember that query-only features can only matter through interactions.

courseTitle: Ranking metrics: precision@k, recall@k, NDCG, MRR
lessonTitle: Is the difference real? Paired tests, effect sizes, many systems
md: Compare systems on per-query differences, with a paired t-test or randomization test, and report the mean difference with a confidence interval and effect size. With many systems, control the familywise error instead of running dozens of independent tests.

courseTitle: Real-time multiplayer networking: WebSockets and state sync
lessonTitle: WebSocket: one HTTP upgrade, then a two-way framed stream
md: Masking is **not encryption**: the key travels in the same frame. RFC 6455 requires it (even over TLS) so that a script in the browser cannot choose the exact bytes on the wire. Without it, an attacker could craft upgraded traffic that a broken proxy reads as an HTTP request and caches, the cache-poisoning attack in section 10.3. Use `wss://` (TLS) for confidentiality.

courseTitle: Recommender systems and cold start
lessonTitle: From a sparse rating matrix to item-to-item recommendations
md: Treating a blank as a rating of 0 is a modelling choice, not a fact. It makes plain cosine reward items that are merely *rated by the same people*, whatever the ratings. In Sarwar et al.'s MovieLens experiments, adjusted cosine gave lower error (MAE) than plain cosine or Pearson correlation.

courseTitle: Recommender systems and cold start
lessonTitle: Evaluating recommenders without fooling yourself
md: Split by time, exclude what the user already consumed, beat tuned simple baselines, and confirm with an online experiment.

courseTitle: Relational operators: joins, aggregation and planning
lessonTitle: Aggregation and sorting: running state, hash tables and spills
md: A GROUP BY result from a HashAggregate has no defined order. If you need sorted output, write ORDER BY; do not rely on the order you happened to see.

courseTitle: Reward hacking: when optimizing the score breaks the task
lessonTitle: When a high score stops meaning a solved task
md: Misconception: reward hacking means the RL algorithm is buggy. DeepMind's analysis points the other way: the behavior comes from misspecification, and a *better* optimizer is more likely to find an intricate loophole that a weaker one would miss. Stronger RL makes the specification matter more, not less.

courseTitle: RL post-training infrastructure at scale
lessonTitle: One RL step is five workloads on two kinds of engine
md: A common misconception is that a bigger training cluster speeds up RL roughly linearly. Training is often a minority of the step. If generation is two-thirds of the time, even infinitely fast training saves at most a third.

courseTitle: Roofline model and GPU bandwidth measurement
lessonTitle: Measuring achieved bandwidth with a copy kernel
md:
Common traps:
- **Arrays that fit in L2.** An 8 MB array on an H100 (50 MB L2) measures cache bandwidth, not HBM.
- **Mixing GB and GiB.** 2,982.6 GB/s is 2,777.8 GiB/s. Use one divisor for both theory and measurement.
- **Timing the first launch** or using host timers without synchronizing.
- **Uncoalesced or strided access**, which measures your access pattern, not the memory.

courseTitle: Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)
lessonTitle: Why fuse ranks instead of scores
md: RRF needs only positions. Scores on different scales, scores that drift between index versions, even systems that expose no scores at all can be fused, because $1/(k + r)$ is the same function of rank for every input.

courseTitle: Rust in the Linux kernel: safe abstractions over unsafe C
lessonTitle: Bindings, helpers, abstractions: the layers under a Rust driver
md: Unsafe code is concentrated in reviewed subsystem abstractions. A driver written only against those abstractions cannot cause undefined behavior, *provided the abstractions are sound* and every `unsafe` block honours its contract. That proviso is the whole game; lesson 6 shows what happens when it fails.

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: Dispatch queues: how tasks travel from BPF to a CPU
md: Inserting a task into a local DSQ is a commitment. Once there, it waits for that CPU even if another CPU goes idle a microsecond later. Schedulers that want work sharing keep tasks in a shared custom DSQ and move them to a local DSQ only when a CPU asks via `ops.dispatch()`.

courseTitle: Self-play and self-improvement: how models learn from their own output
lessonTitle: Why a model can teach itself: improve, then distill
md: A common misconception: self-play means no external signal. Games have a perfect, free judge: the rules decide who won. Take that away and a model playing against itself only amplifies its own beliefs, which is the collapse setting from the prerequisite course.

courseTitle: SGLang: RadixAttention, cache-aware scheduling, compressed FSMs
lessonTitle: RadixAttention: matching, splitting and evicting prefixes
md: A shared prefix is not pinned. It is protected only while running requests hold it or while cached descendants keep it an inner node. Once it becomes a leaf it competes on recency like any other leaf. The current docs offer other scorings (`lfu`, `slru`, `priority`) through `--radix-eviction-policy`; `lru` is the default.

courseTitle: Shortest-path routing on road graphs
lessonTitle: A*: steering the search with a lower bound
md: In practice the straight-line bound is weak on real road networks with travel times: it must divide by the top motorway speed, so it badly underestimates slow city streets. The Bast et al. survey reports the gain is small or nonexistent. **ALT** gets much better bounds from precomputed distances to a few landmarks plus the triangle inequality.

courseTitle: Signal processing basics: sampling, the FFT and filters
lessonTitle: The FFT: from N squared to N log N with butterflies
md: The FFT is not an approximation. It returns the same numbers as the DFT matrix product, up to floating point rounding, by sharing work through $\log_2 N$ stages of $N/2$ butterflies.

courseTitle: SIMD: AVX2, AVX-512, Arm Neon and SVE from the lanes up
lessonTitle: Arm Neon and SVE: fixed width versus length agnostic
md: Misconception: "SVE code is written for a particular width like 512 bits." VLA code must never assume a length; use svcntw() and whilelt. ACLE warns that something like `svptrue_pat_b32(SV_VL16)` loads no data at all on chips narrower than 512 bits.

courseTitle: Slab, bump/arena and buddy allocators
lessonTitle: How Linux stacks them, and how to choose
md: A pool or arena that never returns memory looks like a leak from the outside. Bonwick's caches give memory back under VM pressure; your custom pool should have some way to shrink (reset, trim, or a size cap).

courseTitle: slime: RL post-training with Megatron and SGLang
lessonTitle: Fully async rollout and the price of staleness
md: Fully async needs separate rollout and training GPUs to overlap anything, and its README lists no evaluation mode (it would conflict with the continuously running model), so evaluate with a separate path or job. Importance-sampling corrections such as TIS help with mismatch, but the docs say they do not justify an unlimited stale queue.

courseTitle: Sparse autoencoders: pulling features out of superposition
lessonTitle: Training at scale: dead latents and feature splitting
md: A latent dying is not the same as a feature being absent from the model. It only means this SAE found no use for that column, often because of optimisation, not because the concept is missing.

courseTitle: Spatial interpolation: IDW, variograms and kriging
lessonTitle: Ordinary kriging: solving for the best weights
md: Kriging weights come from solving a linear system, not from a fixed formula. That lets them account for redundancy between sensors (declustering) and for sensors hidden behind others (screening), and it yields an error variance for every estimate.

courseTitle: Speculative decoding: draft fast, verify in one pass, lose nothing
lessonTitle: Speculative sampling: guesses that keep the target's distribution
md: Accept with $\min(1, p/q)$, on rejection sample from $\text{norm}(\max(0, p - q))$. Accepted mass is $\min(p, q)$ and residual mass is $p - \min(p, q)$; they add up to $p$ for any draft.

courseTitle: Speech-to-text: log-mel features, Whisper, CTC and WER
lessonTitle: Word error rate: alignments, normalization and fair comparisons
md: Only compare WER numbers computed with the same normalizer on the same references. Switching normalizers, or counting *you're* versus *you are* as an error, can move WER more than a model upgrade. For languages written without spaces, character error rate (CER) is used instead.

courseTitle: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
lessonTitle: Walking an x86-64 page table, bit by bit
md: Read a pointer as five numbers: four 9-bit table indices and a 12-bit offset. Huge pages simply end the walk early and widen the offset to 21 or 30 bits.

courseTitle: Steering vectors and activation engineering
lessonTitle: Side effects and how to evaluate a steering vector
md: LLM judges are convenient but not neutral. CAA used GPT-4 to score open-ended answers from 1 to 10 and notes the scores are sensitive to the rubric's wording; they spot-checked against their own ratings. String-matching refusal detectors have the opposite problem: they catch "I'm sorry" but not a harmful reply, so Arditi et al. paired them with Llama Guard 2.

courseTitle: Streaming sensor pipelines: event time, watermarks, online filters
lessonTitle: Downsampling, retention and exactly-once vs at-least-once
md: End-to-end exactly-once needs three parts: a replayable source (Kafka offsets), consistent state (checkpoints), and an output that is transactional or idempotent (upsert by a deterministic key such as sensor and window). Duplicates created upstream, such as MQTT QoS 1 retries, must be removed by id.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: Positional encoding, residuals and the full Transformer
md: A Transformer layer = attention (mix across positions) + FFN (transform each position), each wrapped in a residual connection and LayerNorm, with positional information added once at the input.

courseTitle: BM25: saturating, length-normalized term weighting
lessonTitle: BM25 in Lucene and Elasticsearch: fields, tuning, limits
md: BM25 only matches the terms you typed, after analysis. A document saying "low-cost airfare" scores 0 for cheap flights. Synonyms, stemming, query expansion, or a dense (embedding) retriever are needed for vocabulary mismatch, which is why many systems combine BM25 with vector search.

courseTitle: Build a GPT from scratch
lessonTitle: Generating text: the sampling loop, temperature and top-k
md: The model never stores the text it generated anywhere except in `idx`. There is no hidden memory across calls: anything older than `block_size` tokens is simply cropped away and cannot influence the next prediction.

courseTitle: Calculus and gradients: from slopes to backpropagation
lessonTitle: Gradient descent: walking downhill and choosing the step size
md: The gradient gives the direction; the learning rate decides the distance. The largest stable learning rate is set by the **steepest** direction of the loss, while progress in the **shallowest** direction decides how long training takes.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: how bash really runs your commands
lessonTitle: Exit statuses and scripts that fail loudly
md: `set -e` is a safety net, not error handling. It misses failures inside functions called from conditions and in `&&` chains. For steps that matter, check explicitly: `if ! cp src dst; then echo 'copy failed' >&2; exit 1; fi`.

courseTitle: GPU and inference basics
lessonTitle: Inside a GPU: many small cores fed by one big memory
md: A GPU is a throughput machine. It hides slow memory by keeping many warps in flight, not by making any single access fast. Give it too little parallel work and the SMs sit idle.

courseTitle: GPU and inference basics
lessonTitle: Batching: sharing each weight read across many users
md: Bigger batches are not free for users: once the step leaves the flat region (math roof, or growing KV reads), every sequence's inter-token latency rises. A throughput number without a latency number hides this.

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: Why memory is slow and how caches hide it
md: Performance is often decided by memory access patterns, not instruction counts. Touch memory sequentially, reuse data while it is still in cache, and keep hot data small.

courseTitle: How LLMs are trained: pretraining, SFT, RLHF
lessonTitle: Reward models: turning human comparisons into a score
md: The reward model learns only from differences. Its job is to rank responses to the same prompt, and its output is a log-odds score: a gap of 1 means about 73 percent preference.

courseTitle: Inverted indexes and TF-IDF: how keyword search works
lessonTitle: TF-IDF: weighting by frequency and rarity
md: tf rewards a term repeated inside the document; idf rewards a term that is rare across the collection. TF-IDF multiplies them, so a match counts most when the term is frequent here and rare elsewhere.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Addresses and pointers: what int *p actually stores
md: A pointer is a variable whose value is an address. `&` takes an address, `*` follows one, and the pointer's type decides how many bytes are read or written at that address.

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: Who frees this memory? Ownership and drop
md: Ownership is not about the stack versus the heap as such. A `String` header can live on the stack, in a `Vec`, or inside a struct field; wherever it lives, that location is the owner, and the heap block is freed when that owner is dropped.

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: A vector is a list of numbers and an arrow at the same time
md: Adding vectors of different dimensions is undefined in math. NumPy and PyTorch will sometimes *broadcast* (silently repeat) a smaller array to fit, so shape bugs can produce a result instead of an error. Always know the shape of every array you add.

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: Where it shows up: linear layers, batches and attention scores
md: Shape errors are the most common bug in ML code. Before running a line like `X @ W.T + b`, write the shapes next to it, `(B,n) @ (n,m) + (m,)`, and check that inner sizes match and the bias length equals the output size.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Fighting overfitting: validation, weight decay, early stopping
md: With adaptive optimizers the two forms of the penalty differ. Adding $\lambda\lVert w\rVert^2$ to the loss and decaying weights directly are equivalent for plain SGD (after rescaling by the learning rate) but **not** for Adam, which is why AdamW decouples weight decay from the gradient step (Loshchilov and Hutter).

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Processes and limited direct execution
md: Limited direct execution: let the program run natively, but first set up the hardware (trap table, timer, user mode) so that the OS always gets control back. A system call is the voluntary way back in; the timer interrupt is the involuntary one.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Probability by counting outcomes, and what conditioning does
md: Independent is not the same as mutually exclusive. Mutually exclusive events ("sum is 2" and "sum is 12") cannot both happen, so learning one happened tells you the other did not: they are strongly *dependent*. Independence means the joint probability factorizes, $P(A \cap C) = P(A)P(C)$.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Confidence intervals, p-values and an A/B test
md: The American Statistical Association's 2016 statement lists the usual misreadings. A p-value is **not** the probability that $H_0$ is true (that is the Bayes' rule mix-up from lesson 2), it does **not** measure the size or importance of an effect, and decisions should not rest only on whether it crosses 0.05. Report the effect size and its confidence interval.

courseTitle: Scaling laws: predicting loss from model size, data and compute
lessonTitle: Inference cost, overtraining and where scaling laws break
md: Chinchilla-optimal answers one question: lowest loss per training FLOP. Real decisions also weigh inference volume, available data and downstream metrics, so production models are often smaller and trained on far more than 20 tokens per parameter.

courseTitle: Search evaluation basics: precision, recall, MAP, MRR and nDCG
lessonTitle: Comparing systems honestly: judgment holes, variance, online tests
md: A test collection is a measuring instrument with known biases. Report the metric, cutoff and gain you used, look at per-query results, test significance with paired tests, and be suspicious when a genuinely new kind of system loses on an old pool.

courseTitle: Tokenization with Byte Pair Encoding (BPE)
lessonTitle: Why language models read subwords, not words or characters
md: A subword tokenizer gives you short sequences for common text **and** no unknown words, because anything rare can always fall back to smaller pieces. Byte Pair Encoding (BPE) is the most widely used way to choose those pieces.

courseTitle: Training deep nets in practice: init, optimizers, schedules, debugging
lessonTitle: Initialization: keeping signals alive through 30 layers
md: He et al. report that their 30-layer plain ReLU network trained with He initialization while the Xavier-initialized version *completely stalled*, with all gradients diminishing. Yet on their 22-layer model both converged (He init just started reducing error earlier), and on a smaller model the final accuracies were about the same. A bad init does not always crash; past some depth it silently stops learning.

courseTitle: Vector search and ANN: how HNSW finds neighbors fast
lessonTitle: Greedy search on a proximity graph, and why ef matters
md: Greedy graph search has no guarantee of exactness on a real (non-Delaunay) graph. Even a large $ef$ can miss a neighbor if the graph has no path that improves toward it. Recall comes from how well the graph is built, which is the subject of the next two lessons.

courseTitle: Synthetic data and model collapse
lessonTitle: Replace versus accumulate: what keeps the error bounded
md: The question is not whether synthetic data enter the loop, but whether real data stay in it. Keep the original human data, keep adding fresh real data, and treat synthetic data as an addition.

courseTitle: System calls and mmap
lessonTitle: When mmap wins, when it hurts, and how to steer it
md: `MAP_FIXED` forcibly replaces whatever is already mapped at that address. In a multithreaded program another thread (or a library calling `dlopen` or `malloc`) may have just mapped something there, and you silently destroy it. mmap(2) recommends `MAP_FIXED_NOREPLACE`, which fails with `EEXIST` instead of clobbering.

courseTitle: Temporal reasoning: years of experience and current roles
lessonTitle: Why summing job durations overstates experience
md: Common misconception: an LLM can read the resume and state the years of experience. Benchmarks say otherwise. On TimeQA, the best long-document QA model reached 46% accuracy versus 87% for humans, and on Test of Time, frontier LLMs answered only 13.5% to 16% of date *duration* questions correctly. Lesson 5 covers why and what to do instead.

courseTitle: Test-time compute scaling: sampling, search and thinking longer
lessonTitle: Two ways to spend more compute on one prompt
md: Test-time compute is not free at serving time. Every extra sample or thinking token is paid on every request, by every user. Training compute is paid once. That asymmetry decides when test-time scaling is worth it.

courseTitle: Test-time training and learned memory: TTT layers and Titans
lessonTitle: A hidden state that is itself a model you train while reading
md: A TTT layer is an RNN whose hidden state is a model. Update rule = train on the current token. Output rule = predict with the updated model. Choosing the model, the loss and the optimizer chooses the layer.

courseTitle: Thread caches and magazines
lessonTitle: The magazine: a per-CPU stack of object pointers
md: Per-CPU does not automatically mean scalable. The paper found that padding and aligning each CPU's structure to its own cache line was critical for linear scaling. Without it, the per-CPU counters of neighbouring CPUs share a line and you are back to cache line ping-pong (false sharing).

courseTitle: Tiered memory: placing pages across DRAM, CXL and SSD
lessonTitle: The SSD tier, zswap, and running tiering in production
md: CXL can hold *warm* data because a miss there costs about 2x DRAM. Swap can only hold *cold* data because a miss there costs about 100x to 400x. That is why demotion tries CXL first and swap last.

courseTitle: Triton kernels: block-level GPU programming
lessonTitle: From threads to blocks: the Triton programming model
md: A Triton program instance is not one thread. It is closer to a CUDA thread block: one program becomes `num_warps` warps of 32 threads each, so with the default `num_warps=4` a single program runs on 128 threads.

courseTitle: Unified multimodal models: one transformer that reads and draws
lessonTitle: Attention masks for mixed text and image sequences
md: The rule that keeps any mask honest: a position may only attend to what will exist when it is generated. Bidirectional attention inside an image is legal exactly when the whole image is produced together, as in diffusion, flow or masked prediction. Under token-by-token generation it would leak the answer.

courseTitle: Unikernels: one application, one address space, one VM image
lessonTitle: Syscalls become function calls: one address space, one privilege level
md: Running an unmodified binary on a unikernel does not get you function-call costs. Trapping and translating each `syscall` cost 84 cycles in Unikraft's measurement, 21 times a function call. Relinking against the libOS is what removes the crossing.

courseTitle: Vector database internals: SIMD kernels, segments and disk
lessonTitle: Graph traversal: memory layout, cache misses and prefetching
md: Deleting from hnswlib with `markDelete` only sets a flag. The node keeps its edges and is still used for routing; it is just filtered out of results. Lots of deletions therefore still cost traversal time until the index is rebuilt.

courseTitle: verl: the HybridFlow RL training stack for LLMs
lessonTitle: One GRPO step through RayPPOTrainer, call by call
md: Read the source, not just the prose. The reward-function doc says the GSM8K scorer gives 0.1 for a well-formatted wrong answer, but in the current `gsm8k.py` the default `format_score` is 0.0. A silent difference like that changes what the policy is rewarded for.

courseTitle: Video-LLMs with long-video memory
lessonTitle: Bigger context or captions: LongVA, Gemini 1.5, retrieval, benchmarks
md: Choose by the question. Sparse sampling plus pooling suits gist questions. Merging and memory banks suit streaming and bounded memory. Long context gives the most faithful view at the highest cost. Caption retrieval is cheapest per question and reuses work across questions, but only knows what the captioner wrote.

courseTitle: Fine-tuning a vision model (ViT)
lessonTitle: A new head and a higher resolution
md: The longer sequence costs compute. Linear layers scale with token count, so 577 vs 197 tokens is about 2.9x more work per layer, while the attention score matrix grows with the square, about $(577/197)^2 \approx 8.6$x. Simplified: real step time also depends on kernels and memory traffic. Higher-resolution fine-tuning trades accuracy for a large jump in cost.

courseTitle: Vision-language-action models: RT-2, OpenVLA and pi0
lessonTitle: pi0: denoising a whole action chunk with flow matching
md: pi0 replaces "decode 7 tokens per step" with "run a 300M expert 10 times per chunk". Cost no longer grows with the number of action dimensions or the control rate, and the output is continuous.

courseTitle: vLLM attention backends: selection, batching, KV layout, CUDA graphs
lessonTitle: One attention layer, many kernels: the backend abstraction
md: A backend is mostly a *declaration*: what it supports, plus two factories. Selection, batching, KV layout and CUDA graph capture are all driven by those declarations, so a backend never needs to know about the scheduler.

courseTitle: Vision-language models for reading images
lessonTitle: Turning an image into tokens a language model can read
md: Misconception: the model "sees" the image at full resolution. It sees whatever grid the encoder produced. A 4000 x 3000 phone photo squeezed into 336 x 336 loses most of its pixels before the language model ever runs.

courseTitle: Wait-free algorithms: bounded progress for every thread
lessonTitle: Why a lock-free CAS loop can starve one thread
md: The progress ladder, weakest to strongest: **blocking** (a stalled lock holder can stop everyone), **lock-free** (some thread always completes), **wait-free** (every thread completes in finitely many of its own steps), **bounded wait-free** (every thread completes within a fixed number of its own steps).

courseTitle: Weather and climate foundation models: GraphCast to Aurora
lessonTitle: Why learn the weather from 80 years of reanalysis
md: A common misconception is that these models learn from raw observations. They learn to imitate ERA5, so they inherit its biases (GraphCast excludes precipitation from its headline evaluation because ERA5 precipitation has known biases), and they start each forecast from an NWP analysis.

courseTitle: Work stealing and thread pools
lessonTitle: Why a pool needs more than one shared queue
md: Work stealing moves the cost of load balancing onto idle workers. Busy workers pay almost nothing; the worker with nothing to do is the one that goes looking.

courseTitle: Zero-copy I/O: sendfile, splice and MSG_ZEROCOPY
lessonTitle: Where the copies go in a read and write loop
md: Zero-copy means removing the **CPU copies between the page cache, user memory and socket buffers**. Device DMA still happens. The win scales with bytes moved, so it matters when a program mostly shovels data it does not inspect.

courseTitle: Zero-copy I/O: sendfile, splice and MSG_ZEROCOPY
lessonTitle: When zero-copy pays: measurements, limits and choices
md: Common failure modes: modifying a buffer or file before the kernel is done with it (silent corruption on the wire), forgetting to drain the error queue (pinned memory grows until ENOBUFS), benchmarking over loopback (always copied), and assuming a notification means the peer received the data.
